lead: Every phone runs an operating system: the layer that owns the hardware and lends it to apps. It decides which app gets the CPU, which is killed when memory runs short, which may read your contacts, and which may be installed at all. That last power makes the OS a shopkeeper as well as a manager. Pick Android, iOS or the retired Windows Phone and you also pick a language, a build tool and a store. This chapter compares the three, with Android in the most detail, because the rest of this unit builds on it.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for what a cellular network and a data connection do; nothing else.

sections.h3: What a mobile OS actually does

blocks.text: A mobile operating system (OS) is the software layer between the phone's hardware and the apps on the screen. When you hold the power button, the OS starts, checks the hardware and shows the home screen. From then on it hands out CPU time, memory, storage and radio access to every app that asks.
Four jobs define a phone OS.

items: Process and memory management. Each app runs as one or more processes, and the OS gives each process a private memory area. A phone has little RAM, so when a new app needs memory the OS quietly kills a background app and restarts it later from saved state.
Power management. The battery is the hard limit. The OS sleeps the CPU when nothing needs it, slows the clock under light load, and freezes background apps so they cannot drain the battery.

Sandboxing and permissions. Each app is boxed in. Android gives every app its own Linux user id (uid), so the file system itself blocks it from other apps' files. iOS uses its own sandbox for the same purpose. Anything outside the box — camera, contacts, location, microphone — needs a permission the user grants at run time.
Install, update and payment. The OS decides what code may be installed and who must have signed it. On Android and iOS that means an app store; on Windows Phone it meant the Microsoft Store.

blocks.text: This is why the OS choice is a business decision, not a detail. It fixes your language, your tools and how you get paid.

sections.h3: Android, iOS and Windows Phone side by side

blocks.text: Android sits on the Linux kernel, but it is not a Linux distribution in the Ubuntu sense: a retail phone has no shell package manager, and the framework you touch is Google's code. Above the kernel lie a hardware abstraction layer, native C and C++ libraries, the Android Runtime (ART) that executes an app's DEX bytecode, and the Java API framework. Apps are written in Java or Kotlin; Kotlin is Google's preferred language now. The core is open source as the Android Open Source Project, and most retail phones add Google Play services — Maps, push messaging, the Play Store — under licence.

iOS runs on the Darwin kernel (Mach and BSD code), is closed source, and ships only on Apple hardware. Apps use Swift, or the older Objective-C, and are built in Xcode. Xcode runs only on macOS, so an iOS build needs a Mac. Installation is through the App Store alone.

Windows Phone used C# and XAML on the .NET stack, built in Visual Studio, with a tile-based interface called Metro or Modern UI. Microsoft stopped developing it, so treat it as history, next to BlackBerry's QNX-based system. Some syllabi group these under 'commercial mobile operating systems'.

sections.h3: From source code to a paid download

blocks.text: The path from source code to a download is the same shape on every platform.

items: Write the code in the platform language.
Declare what the app needs: Android lists permissions in AndroidManifest.xml; iOS states usage reasons in its Info.plist.
Build and sign. Gradle produces a signed APK or AAB with your key; Xcode signs with your certificate and provisioning profile.
Distribute. The store reviews the build and publishes it.
Bill. The store charges the buyer, keeps its commission and remits the rest to you.

blocks.text: That last step is where m-commerce enters. An in-app purchase is charged to the user's stored card through the store's billing, and the developer is paid monthly. Selling physical goods may use an outside gateway such as UPI instead, which is why checkout rules differ between app categories. See Unit 5 for the publishing and checkout flow.

spec.title: Same to-do app, three platforms, two that ship
spec.aria: A flow chart where one to-do app branches into Android, iOS and Windows Phone builds, the three merge into the count 3 minus 1 equals 2 living platforms, and two builds ship.

examples.question: A small team must ship the same to-do app on Android, iOS and Windows Phone. For each platform, state the main language, the build tool, the store, and the one extra requirement. Then state how many of the three platforms the app actually ships on.
steps: Android: language Java or Kotlin; build tool Android Studio with Gradle; store Google Play; extra requirement none — any Windows, macOS or Linux PC will build it.
iOS: language Swift or Objective-C; build tool Xcode; store the App Store; extra requirement a Mac running macOS, because Xcode runs nowhere else.

Windows Phone: language C# with XAML for the interface; build tool Visual Studio; store the Microsoft Store; extra requirement none, but the platform is no longer developed, so there are no new devices and no new users to win.
Count the platforms that are still living: Android and iOS are developed, Windows Phone is retired. Living platforms = 3 − 1 = 2.
So the to-do app is written twice, in Java/Kotlin and in Swift, and the third build is dropped.
examples.answer: Two of the three platforms ship: Android in Java or Kotlin built with Gradle for Google Play, and iOS in Swift built in Xcode on a Mac for the App Store; Windows Phone (C#, XAML, Visual Studio) is retired.
examples.check:
platforms = ["Android", "iOS", "Windows Phone"]
developed = {"Android": True, "iOS": True, "Windows Phone": False}
print(len(platforms))
print(sum(1 for p in platforms if developed[p]))

traps: Writing that Android is a Linux distribution in the Ubuntu sense. Only the kernel is Linux; the framework, ART and Play services above it are Google's.
Quoting a platform version without its API level. Android 13 is API level 33, and the API level is what decides whether a call compiles.
Mixing up ART and Dalvik. Dalvik was the older Android runtime; ART replaced it and is what executes app bytecode today.
Mixing up Windows Phone with Windows Mobile. They are separate products, and Windows Mobile is the older one.
Claiming Xcode runs on Windows. It does not, so any iOS build and signing job needs a Mac.

quiz.q: Name the kernel under Android and the kernel under iOS.
quiz.a: Android uses the Linux kernel. iOS uses the Darwin kernel, built from Mach and BSD code.

quiz.q: Which runtime executes an Android app's DEX bytecode?
Why does sandboxing limit the damage a malicious app can do?
quiz.a: Each app runs under its own user id and private storage, so the OS blocks it from reading other apps' files. To reach the camera, contacts or location it must ask for a permission the user can deny.

quiz.q: Why is 'Android is a Linux distribution' a wrong statement?
quiz.a: Only the kernel comes from Linux. The libraries, ART, the Java API framework and the Play Store are Google's, and a retail phone has no Linux package manager or shell tools.

quiz.q: An Android app needs the camera and the contacts list. Where is each need declared, and when is it granted?
quiz.a: Both are declared in AndroidManifest.xml. Both are then requested at run time and granted by the user through a permission dialog; the app must handle a refusal.

quiz.q: A five-person team owns only Windows laptops and must build for Android and iOS. What is the smallest sensible hardware purchase, and why?
quiz.a: One Mac. The Mac builds and signs the iOS app in Xcode and can also build the Android app; the Windows laptops cannot run Xcode at all.

quiz.q: A client asks for a new Windows Phone app to reach 'a less crowded store'. Give two reasons to refuse and one alternative.
quiz.a: The platform is no longer developed, so no new devices or users arrive, and the build and store chain will not be supported long term. The effort is better spent on Android and iOS, or on a cross-platform build that covers both.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most teams now write one codebase in Flutter or React Native, ship it to both stores, and drop into Swift or Kotlin only for camera, Bluetooth and other platform-specific work. Regulators in some regions now require phone makers to allow third-party app stores, which weakens the store-as-gatekeeper model described above. On-device machine learning and tighter privacy rules are pushing more processing onto the phone itself. Search for Flutter, React Native, AOSP versus Google Play services, and the Digital Markets Act app-store rules.
